name: Mandibular advancement device

lead: A mandibular advancement device is a custom mouthpiece worn at night that holds the lower jaw slightly forward to keep the airway open. People with snoring or sleep apnea use it to sleep better, which feeds into a more rested look.

Holding the lower jaw forward widens the airway behind the tongue during sleep. Its evidence is for snoring and obstructive sleep apnea: professional sleep societies recommend it for primary snoring and for people who cannot tolerate CPAP, and a randomised trial compared it with CPAP in severe apnea. No studies in the sources reviewed examine appearance effects.

paras: A dentist fits a custom splint that is worn each night, usually after a sleep assessment. People who can't tolerate CPAP often turn to it, and follow-up visits adjust the fit.
Dry mouth, tooth and jaw soreness and lasting changes in how the teeth meet are reported. It is a prescription medical device.

angle.text: A mandibular advancement device keeps the airway open during sleep, cutting snoring and apnea so you sleep better and look more rested. It is a medical device studied for sleep apnea, with no published research on appearance.

lead: A mandibular advancement device (MAD) is a custom-made oral appliance worn during sleep that holds the lower jaw slightly forward, used mainly to treat snoring and obstructive sleep apnea [1]. It is a medical device rather than a cosmetic one, and the sources reviewed describe no published research on appearance effects.

Reviews describe CPAP as the recommended first-line treatment for obstructive sleep apnea, with MADs among alternatives that have promising data but limited strong evidence. Wikipedia reports that professional sleep societies recommend MADs for primary snoring and for people who cannot tolerate CPAP [1]. A randomised trial has compared a MAD against CPAP in severe obstructive sleep apnea [2], and a systematic review has examined how device design affects outcomes [3].
infobox: Dry mouth, tooth and jaw discomfort, bite changes [1]

paras: The appliance fits over the teeth and advances the lower jaw, which enlarges the airway behind the tongue during sleep. Wikipedia describes it as noninvasive, reversible and quiet [1].

Wikipedia reports that MADs tend to work better for mild and moderate apnea than for severe apnea, that they were found comparable to CPAP in lowering blood pressure, and that patients often found CPAP more effective but the splint easier to use [1]. A review of OSA treatments notes that MADs, positional therapy and hypoglossal nerve stimulation are alternatives with encouraging data but little strong evidence.

Dry mouth, tooth pain and jaw discomfort are common, and many users stop because of discomfort or poor results. Long-term use was not linked to temporomandibular disorders but was associated with permanent changes in how the teeth meet [1].
The sources reviewed contain no looksmaxxing community discussion of MADs as an appearance tool, and no studies of facial-appearance effects.

Studies concern sleep apnea, not appearance. A randomised comparison of MAD and CPAP in severe obstructive sleep apnea has been published [2], and a meta-analysis has reviewed MAD design and outcomes [3]. No studies found on appearance outcomes.
